children.title: What's An Owner to Do?
children.summary: It's a good time to own a ship that needs scrapping. With rates reaching $400 per ton, and in some cases even higher, the industry has never seen such high prices paid for scrap vessels.

children.title: Chart: Scrap Prices vs Steel Prices
section_path: Chart: Scrap Prices vs Steel Prices
children.section_path_text: Chart: Scrap Prices vs Steel Prices
children.summary: Scrap Prices and WS Rates Neck in Neck Historically, owners have scrapped vessels when Worldscale (WS) rates are low, and have kept ships afloat when rates are robust. As shown on the next page, owners are now facing a difficult decision.

children.title: Chart: Scrap Prices Vs WS Rates
section_path: Chart: Scrap Prices Vs WS Rates
children.section_path_text: Chart: Scrap Prices Vs WS Rates
children.summary: When Tonnage is Low, Scrap Prices are High One conclusion we can draw from the graph below is that the lack of available vessels for scrapping is also driving prices up. Since spot market rates are so high right now, this is a logical conclusion.

children.title: Chart: Scrap Prices vs LDT Scrapped
section_path: Chart: Scrap Prices vs LDT Scrapped
children.section_path_text: Chart: Scrap Prices vs LDT Scrapped
children.summary: The chart below shows that scrapping activity does inversely follow tanker rates. Scrapping activity tends to rise when tanker rates are low and vice-versa.

children.title: What to Do?
children.summary: While scrap prices are high, tanker owners with older tonnage are probably wise to keep trading in the spot market. But at the slightest sign of weakness, grab $400/ton and run with it.
